notes.definition: Eukaryotic cells (plant and animal cells) have a cell membrane, cytoplasm and genetic material enclosed in a nucleus. Prokaryotic cells (bacteria) are much smaller and their genetic material is not enclosed in a nucleus: it is a single loop of DNA, often with extra small rings of DNA called plasmids.
explanation: All living things are made of cells, and every cell falls into one of two groups. Eukaryotic cells are the cells that make up plants, animals, fungi and protists. They all have a cell membrane, cytoplasm and genetic material that is enclosed in a nucleus. The word eukaryotic means 'true nucleus'. Prokaryotic cells are bacterial cells. The word prokaryotic means 'before nucleus', which is a useful way to remember that bacteria do not have one.

A bacterial cell has cytoplasm and a cell membrane, and the cell membrane is surrounded by a cell wall. Its genetic material is not enclosed in a nucleus. Instead, most of the DNA is found as a single loop (a circular chromosome) lying free in the cytoplasm. Many bacteria also have one or more plasmids, which are small extra rings of DNA. Plasmids often carry useful genes, such as genes for resistance to antibiotics, and they can be passed between bacteria. Bacterial cells also contain ribosomes, where proteins are made.

Prokaryotic cells are much smaller than eukaryotic cells. A typical bacterium is about 1 to 5 μm long, a typical animal cell is about 10 to 30 μm across and many plant cells are 10 to 100 μm long. Because cells are so small, biologists measure them in micrometres (μm) and nanometres (nm). 1 mm = 1000 μm and 1 μm = 1000 nm. In metres, 1 μm = 1 × 10⁻⁶ m and 1 nm = 1 × 10⁻⁹ m.

To compare sizes that are very different, scientists use orders of magnitude. Each order of magnitude is a factor of 10. To work out how many orders of magnitude bigger one object is than another, first put both sizes into the same unit, then divide the larger size by the smaller one. If the answer is 10, the difference is one order of magnitude; if it is 100 (10²), it is two orders of magnitude; if it is 1000 (10³), it is three. A plant cell of 100 μm is 100 times, or two orders of magnitude, longer than a bacterium of 1 μm.

Standard form is the clearest way to write very small sizes. A number in standard form is written as A × 10ⁿ, where A is at least 1 but less than 10. For example, 0.000 002 m is written as 2 × 10⁻⁶ m. When you compare two sizes written in standard form with the same first number, you can find the difference in orders of magnitude simply by comparing the powers of ten: 3 × 10⁻⁴ m is two orders of magnitude bigger than 3 × 10⁻⁶ m.
keyFacts: Plant and animal cells are eukaryotic: their genetic material is enclosed in a nucleus.
Bacterial cells are prokaryotic: their genetic material is not enclosed in a nucleus.
All cells have a cell membrane and cytoplasm.
Bacteria have a cell membrane surrounded by a cell wall.
Bacterial DNA is a single loop in the cytoplasm, and there may be one or more plasmids (small rings of DNA).
Bacterial cells are much smaller than eukaryotic cells, typically 1 to 5 μm long.
One order of magnitude is a difference of 10 times; two orders is 100 times; three orders is 1000 times.

keyTerms.definition: A cell whose genetic material is enclosed in a nucleus, such as a plant or animal cell.
A cell whose genetic material is not enclosed in a nucleus, such as a bacterial cell.
A small ring of DNA found in the cytoplasm of many bacterial cells, separate from the main loop of DNA.
The main genetic material of a bacterial cell: one circular molecule of DNA lying free in the cytoplasm.
A rigid layer outside the cell membrane that strengthens the cell. Found in bacterial, plant and algal cells.
A power of ten used to compare sizes. Something ten times bigger is one order of magnitude bigger.
A way of writing numbers as A × 10ⁿ, where A is at least 1 and less than 10, e.g. 2.5 × 10⁻⁶ m.
A unit of length equal to one thousandth of a millimetre, or 1 × 10⁻⁶ m.

workedExamples.title: Writing a cell size in standard form
workedExamples.question: A bacterium is 4 μm long. Write its length in metres using standard form.
steps: 4 is between 1 and 10, so the number is already in standard form.

workedExamples.title: Comparing sizes using orders of magnitude
workedExamples.question: A plant cell is 0.1 mm long. A bacterium is 1 μm long. How many orders of magnitude longer is the plant cell?
steps: Put both sizes in the same unit: 0.1 mm = 0.1 × 1000 = 100 μm.
Divide the larger by the smaller: 100 μm ÷ 1 μm = 100.
100 = 10², so the difference is 2 orders of magnitude.
workedExamples.answer: The plant cell is 2 orders of magnitude (100 times) longer than the bacterium.

workedExamples.title: Using sizes to compare cells
workedExamples.question: How many bacteria, each 2 μm long, could fit end to end across an animal cell 30 μm wide?
steps: Both sizes are already in μm.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think that bacteria have no DNA because they have no nucleus.
misconceptions.right: In fact bacteria do have DNA. It is a single loop lying free in the cytoplasm, often with extra plasmids. It is just not enclosed in a nucleus.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think that having a cell wall means a cell must be a plant cell.
misconceptions.right: In fact bacterial cells and algal cells also have cell walls. The key difference between prokaryotes and eukaryotes is whether the genetic material is enclosed in a nucleus.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think 'two orders of magnitude' means two times bigger.
misconceptions.right: In fact each order of magnitude is a factor of 10, so two orders of magnitude means 10 × 10 = 100 times bigger.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think plasmids are the main genetic material of a bacterium.
misconceptions.right: In fact the main genetic material is the single large loop of DNA. Plasmids are small, extra rings of DNA, and not all bacteria have them.

realWorld: Plasmids can carry genes for antibiotic resistance and can be passed from one bacterium to another, which helps resistance spread through bacterial populations.
Scientists use bacterial plasmids in genetic engineering, for example inserting the human insulin gene into a plasmid so bacteria make insulin for people with diabetes.
Knowing that bacteria are around 1 to 5 μm long explains why filters with very small pores (smaller than 1 μm) can be used to remove bacteria from drinking water.
examTips: When asked how prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells differ, always say that the genetic material in a prokaryotic cell is 'not enclosed in a nucleus'. Saying bacteria 'have no DNA' will lose the mark.
Before comparing sizes, convert both measurements into the same unit. A common mistake is dividing 0.1 mm by 1 μm without converting first.
For order of magnitude questions, divide the larger size by the smaller size, then count the powers of ten: 10 is one order, 100 is two, 1000 is three.
Check that standard form answers have exactly one non-zero digit before the decimal point, for example 2.5 × 10⁻⁶ m, not 25 × 10⁻⁷ m.
If a question asks for structures found in both bacterial and plant cells, give cell membrane, cytoplasm, cell wall or ribosomes. Do not give nucleus or chloroplast.
summary: Eukaryotic cells (plant and animal) have genetic material enclosed in a nucleus.
Prokaryotic cells (bacteria) have no nucleus: a single DNA loop plus possibly plasmids.
Bacteria have a cell membrane, cytoplasm and a cell wall.
Bacterial cells are much smaller than eukaryotic cells.
Each order of magnitude is a factor of 10.

A cell whose genetic material is not enclosed in a nucleus, e.g. a bacterial cell.

flashcards.front: What structures do all cells have?
flashcards.back: A cell membrane and cytoplasm (and genetic material).

flashcards.front: What surrounds the cell membrane of a bacterium?
Describe the genetic material of a bacterium.
flashcards.back: A single loop of DNA free in the cytoplasm, often with one or more plasmids.
A small ring of DNA found in many bacterial cells.

flashcards.front: Which is bigger: a bacterium or an animal cell?
flashcards.back: An animal cell. Bacteria are much smaller (about 1 to 5 μm long).

flashcards.front: How many micrometres are in 1 mm?
How many nanometres are in 1 μm?

questions.question: Which structure is found in many bacterial cells but not in plant or animal cells?
markScheme: 1 mark: plasmid
questions.explanation: Plasmids are small rings of DNA found in many bacteria. Bacteria do not have a nucleus, mitochondria or chloroplasts, so those are features of eukaryotic cells instead.

questions.question: Which of these is a prokaryotic cell?
markScheme: 1 mark: bacterium
questions.explanation: Bacteria are prokaryotes because their genetic material is not enclosed in a nucleus. Cheek, onion and leaf cells are all eukaryotic cells with a nucleus.

questions.question: Cells that have their genetic material enclosed in a nucleus are described as:
markScheme: 1 mark: eukaryotic
questions.explanation: Eukaryotic cells, such as plant and animal cells, have a nucleus. Prokaryotic (bacterial) cells do not. A plasmid is a ring of DNA, not a type of cell.

questions.question: Which statement about the size of bacterial cells is correct?
options: Bacterial cells are much smaller than most plant and animal cells
Bacterial cells are much larger than most plant and animal cells
Bacterial cells are about the same size as most plant cells
Bacterial cells are smaller than a ribosome
markScheme: 1 mark: bacterial cells are much smaller than most plant and animal cells
questions.explanation: Bacteria are typically 1 to 5 μm long, while animal cells are about 10 to 30 μm and plant cells up to about 100 μm. Ribosomes (about 25 nm) are far smaller than a bacterium, and bacteria themselves contain ribosomes.

questions.question: Where is the main genetic material found in a bacterial cell?
options: Attached to the outside of the cell wall
As a single loop of DNA free in the cytoplasm
markScheme: 1 mark: as a single loop of DNA free in the cytoplasm
questions.explanation: Bacteria are prokaryotes, so their DNA is not enclosed in a nucleus. It forms a single loop in the cytoplasm. Bacteria do not have mitochondria, and DNA is not attached to the outside of the wall.

questions.question: Which pair of structures is found in BOTH animal cells and bacterial cells?
markScheme: 1 mark: cell membrane and cytoplasm
questions.explanation: All cells have a cell membrane and cytoplasm. Animal cells have no cell wall and no plasmids, and bacteria have no nucleus, so every other pair includes at least one structure missing from one of the cells.

questions.question: What is 1 μm in metres?
markScheme: 1 mark: 1 × 10⁻⁶ m
questions.explanation: There are 1000 μm in 1 mm and 1000 mm in 1 m, so there are 1 000 000 μm in 1 m. One micrometre is therefore one millionth of a metre, 1 × 10⁻⁶ m. 1 × 10⁻³ m is 1 mm and 1 × 10⁻⁹ m is 1 nm.

questions.question: A plant cell is 80 μm long. A bacterium is 0.8 μm long. How many orders of magnitude longer is the plant cell?
markScheme: 1 mark: 2 orders of magnitude
questions.explanation: 80 ÷ 0.8 = 100, and 100 = 10², so the plant cell is 2 orders of magnitude longer. '100 orders of magnitude' confuses the ratio (100 times) with the number of powers of ten.

questions.question: Which statement about eukaryotic and prokaryotic cells is correct?
options: Both types of cell contain genetic material, but only eukaryotic cells enclose it in a nucleus
Prokaryotic cells are generally larger than eukaryotic cells
Only prokaryotic cells have a cell membrane
Eukaryotic cells never have a cell wall
markScheme: 1 mark: both types of cell contain genetic material, but only eukaryotic cells enclose it in a nucleus
questions.explanation: Every cell has genetic material; the difference is whether it is enclosed in a nucleus. Prokaryotes are smaller, all cells have a cell membrane, and plant cells (which are eukaryotic) do have a cell wall.

questions.question: A bacterium is 0.000 002 5 m long. Which shows this length correctly in standard form?
markScheme: 1 mark: 2.5 × 10⁻⁶ m
questions.explanation: Move the decimal point 6 places to the right to get 2.5, so the power is 10⁻⁶. 25 × 10⁻⁷ m has the same value but is not standard form because 25 is not between 1 and 10. 10⁶ would be a huge length, not a tiny one.

questions.question: A bacterial cell is 3 μm long. What is its length in nanometres?
markScheme: 1 mark: 3000 nm
questions.explanation: 1 μm = 1000 nm, so 3 μm = 3 × 1000 = 3000 nm. To convert from a larger unit to a smaller unit you multiply.

questions.question: An animal cell is 20 μm wide. A bacterium is 2 μm long. How many times bigger is the animal cell than the bacterium?
markScheme: 1 mark: 10 (times)
questions.explanation: Both sizes are in μm, so divide: 20 ÷ 2 = 10. The animal cell is 10 times bigger, which is one order of magnitude.

questions.question:
A plant cell is 1.2 × 10⁻⁴ m long. A bacterium is 1.2 × 10⁻⁶ m long.
Calculate how many orders of magnitude longer the plant cell is than the bacterium.
markScheme: 1 mark: 2 (orders of magnitude)
questions.explanation: Dividing gives 10⁻⁴ ÷ 10⁻⁶ = 10², which is 100 times. 100 is two powers of ten, so the plant cell is 2 orders of magnitude longer. A shortcut: the first numbers are the same, so subtract the powers: -4 - (-6) = 2.

questions.question: A bacterium is 3 μm long. Give its length in metres in standard form. (Enter your answer as a number, e.g. 3e-6.)
markScheme: 1 mark: 3 × 10⁻⁶ m
questions.explanation: 1 μm = 1 × 10⁻⁶ m, so 3 μm = 3 × 10⁻⁶ m (0.000 003 m). A common error is 3 × 10⁻³ m, which is 3 mm.

questions.question: A bacterium is 2 μm long. Calculate how many of these bacteria could fit end to end across a distance of 0.1 mm.
markScheme: 1 mark: converts 0.1 mm to 100 μm
questions.explanation: First convert to the same unit: 0.1 mm × 1000 = 100 μm. Then divide: 100 μm ÷ 2 μm = 50 bacteria. Dividing 0.1 by 2 without converting gives 0.05, which is meaningless here.

questions.question:
A plant cell is 0.1 mm long. A ribosome is 25 nm across.
Calculate how many times longer the plant cell is than the ribosome.
markScheme: 1 mark: converts 0.1 mm to 100 000 nm (or 25 nm to 0.025 μm)
1 mark: 4000
questions.explanation: 0.1 mm = 100 μm = 100 000 nm. Then 100 000 ÷ 25 = 4000. Alternatively, 25 nm = 0.025 μm and 100 ÷ 0.025 = 4000. Both methods must use the same units.

questions.question: Name two structures that are found in both bacterial cells and plant cells.
markScheme: 1 mark each for any two from: cell membrane; cytoplasm; cell wall; ribosomes
Do not accept: nucleus, chloroplast, mitochondria, vacuole
questions.explanation: Both bacterial and plant cells have a cell membrane, cytoplasm, a cell wall and ribosomes. Bacteria do not have a nucleus, chloroplasts, mitochondria or a permanent vacuole.

questions.question: What is a plasmid?
markScheme: 1 mark: a small ring / loop of DNA (found in bacterial cells)
questions.explanation: A plasmid is a small, extra ring of DNA found in the cytoplasm of many bacteria, separate from the main DNA loop.

questions.question: Describe how the genetic material in a prokaryotic cell differs from the genetic material in a eukaryotic cell.
markScheme: 1 mark: in a prokaryotic cell the genetic material is not enclosed in a nucleus (in eukaryotic cells it is)
1 mark: it is a single loop of DNA / it may also include plasmids
questions.explanation: In eukaryotic cells the DNA is inside a nucleus. In prokaryotic cells it is a single loop of DNA free in the cytoplasm, and there may also be plasmids.

questions.question: Give two differences between a bacterial cell and a plant cell.
markScheme: 1 mark each for any two differences, e.g.:
bacterial cell has no nucleus / genetic material not in a nucleus
bacterial cell is much smaller
bacterial cell may have plasmids
bacterial cell has a single loop of DNA
bacterial cell has no chloroplasts / no permanent vacuole / no mitochondria
questions.explanation: The key difference is the lack of a nucleus. Bacteria are also much smaller and may contain plasmids, and they lack chloroplasts, mitochondria and a permanent vacuole. Both have a cell wall, so 'cell wall' is not a difference.

questions.question:
A cell has a cell wall, a cell membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes and a nucleus.
Is this cell prokaryotic or eukaryotic? Explain your answer.
acceptedAnswers: genetic material enclosed in a nucleus
markScheme: 1 mark: eukaryotic
1 mark: because it has a nucleus / its genetic material is enclosed in a nucleus
questions.explanation: The deciding feature is the nucleus. A cell wall does not show it is a prokaryote because plant and algal cells also have cell walls. This could be a plant cell.

questions.question:
A typical animal cell is 2 × 10⁻⁵ m across. A typical bacterium is 2 × 10⁻⁶ m long. A typical plant cell is 1 × 10⁻⁴ m long.
Use orders of magnitude to compare the size of the bacterium with the two eukaryotic cells.
acceptedAnswers: animal cell is one order of magnitude bigger
plant cell is two orders of magnitude bigger
markScheme: 1 mark: animal cell is 10 times / 1 order of magnitude larger than the bacterium
1 mark: plant cell is 50 times larger, about 2 orders of magnitude larger than the bacterium
questions.explanation: 2 × 10⁻⁵ ÷ 2 × 10⁻⁶ = 10, one order of magnitude. 1 × 10⁻⁴ ÷ 2 × 10⁻⁶ = 50; 50 is closer to 100 than 10 on a powers-of-ten scale (log₁₀ 50 ≈ 1.7), so it is about two orders of magnitude. Both eukaryotic cells are much bigger than the prokaryote.

questions.question: Cell X is 0.05 mm long. Cell Y is 40 μm long. Which cell is longer? Show your working.
markScheme: 1 mark: 0.05 mm = 50 μm (or 40 μm = 0.04 mm)
1 mark: cell X is longer
questions.explanation: 0.05 × 1000 = 50 μm, which is larger than 40 μm, so cell X is longer. Comparing 0.05 with 40 without converting units would wrongly suggest cell Y is longer.

questions.question: State the name given to cells, such as bacteria, that do not have their genetic material enclosed in a nucleus.
markScheme: 1 mark: prokaryotic / prokaryotes
questions.explanation: Prokaryotic cells have no nucleus. Eukaryotic cells, such as plant and animal cells, do have a nucleus.

questions.question:
A student writes: 'Bacteria do not have any DNA because they do not have a nucleus.'
Explain why the student is wrong.
acceptedAnswers: DNA needed to control the cell
markScheme: 1 mark: bacteria do have DNA / genetic material
1 mark: it is a single loop of DNA free in the cytoplasm (not enclosed in a nucleus)
1 mark: there may also be plasmids / small rings of DNA
questions.explanation: All cells need genetic material to control their activities. In bacteria the DNA is simply not enclosed in a nucleus: it forms a single loop in the cytoplasm, and there may also be plasmids.

questions.question: Compare the structure of a bacterial cell with the structures of an animal cell and a plant cell.
markScheme: Indicative content:
all three have a cell membrane and cytoplasm
all three contain ribosomes
animal and plant cells are eukaryotic: genetic material enclosed in a nucleus
bacterial cells are prokaryotic: no nucleus
bacterial DNA is a single loop free in the cytoplasm
bacteria may have plasmids; animal and plant cells do not
bacteria and plant cells both have a cell wall; animal cells do not
plant cell wall is made of cellulose
animal and plant cells have mitochondria; bacteria do not
plant cells have chloroplasts and a permanent vacuole; bacteria and animal cells do not
bacterial cells are much smaller (about 1 to 5 μm) than animal or plant cells (about 10 to 100 μm)
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a detailed comparison giving both similarities and differences between the bacterial cell and each eukaryotic cell, including the nucleus/DNA difference and size.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): several valid similarities or differences, including the lack of a nucleus in bacteria.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements about one or two structures, with little comparison.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: A strong answer is a genuine comparison: it states what all three share (membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes), what bacteria lack (nucleus, mitochondria, chloroplasts, vacuole), what bacteria have that eukaryotes do not (plasmids, single DNA loop) and where bacteria match plant cells (cell wall). It also comments on the large size difference.

questions.question:
A textbook gives these typical sizes:
Palisade (leaf) cell: 60 μm
Human cheek cell: 50 μm
Bacterium: 0.6 μm
Ribosome: 0.025 μm
Describe what the data show about the sizes of prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells. Use calculations to support your answer.
markScheme: Indicative content:
the eukaryotic cells (palisade and cheek) are similar in size to each other
the bacterium is much smaller than both eukaryotic cells
palisade cell ÷ bacterium = 60 ÷ 0.6 = 100, so 2 orders of magnitude
cheek cell ÷ bacterium = 50 ÷ 0.6 ≈ 83, about 2 orders of magnitude
the ribosome is much smaller than the bacterium: 0.6 ÷ 0.025 = 24 times
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): clear description of the size differences supported by at least one correct calculation using orders of magnitude.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statement that bacteria are smaller, with no or incorrect calculation.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: The palisade cell is 100 times (two orders of magnitude) longer than the bacterium. The cheek cell is about 83 times bigger, which is also roughly two orders of magnitude. This shows prokaryotic cells are much smaller than eukaryotic cells, while sub-cellular structures such as ribosomes are smaller still.
